summary: This program asks the builder for a house's address, bedroom and bathroom counts, and then for a room-by-room layout, storing each room in a list inside a House object before printing a summary report. It shows how one object (House) can hold a collection of other objects (Room).

lines.text: ArrayList is the resizable list implementation used to collect the rooms as they are typed in, since the number of rooms is not known until the builder says so.
A single Scanner tied to the keyboard is created once and reused for every prompt in the program.
nextLine reads the whole line, which matters here because a street address contains spaces that would break nextWord-style reading.
Bathrooms are stored as a double so that half baths such as 2.5 can be recorded.
This count controls how many times the room-entry loop will run.
After reading a number, the newline the user pressed is still waiting in the buffer; this extra nextLine throws it away so the next nextLine reads real text instead of an empty string.
The variable is declared as the List interface but built as an ArrayList, a common Java habit that keeps the code flexible about the exact list type.
Counting from 1 up to roomCount means the prompts read naturally as "room 1", "room 2", and so on.
The room's purpose may be two words, such as "Living Room", so the full line is read.
The three values just gathered are bundled into one Room object and appended to the list, so related data travels together instead of as three loose variables.

lines.code: House house = new House(address, bedrooms, bathrooms);
lines.text: The house itself is created only after all its basic facts are known, passing them straight to the constructor.
The finished list of rooms is handed to the House, making the layout part of the object's state.
Reporting is delegated to a separate method so main stays focused on gathering input.
The method is private because only this class needs it, and static because it is called from main without an instance of HouseBuilder.
Asking the list for its size gives the room count without needing to store that number separately.
The enhanced for loop walks every Room in the list in the order it was entered.
Each room prints its own stored details through its getters, which is the object-oriented alternative to juggling parallel arrays of names and sizes.
